episodes.title: Agents That Self Improve While You Sleep - Fuad Ali, Arize AI
episodes.description:
In this workshop, Fuad Ali of Arize AI shows how to build a self-improvement loop for AI agents: trace everything, let Signal (an always-on agent) read your traces on a schedule and file deduplicated issues, turn failures into evals and living regression datasets, run experiments to prove a fix works, and keep humans at the highest-leverage points: eval design, dataset curation and reviewing fixes. He demos the loop on a toy-shopping agent with a planted bug and takes questions on evaluating qualitative output, decision models and cost.

episodes.title: How to Test Your Agents on Real Tasks With Harbor - Xander Song, Arize AI
episodes.description:
Xander Song, an engineer at Arize AI who works on Phoenix, introduces Harbor, an open source framework for evaluating agents on realistic tasks with real data in isolated sandboxes. He explains tasks, Docker environments, verifiers and rewards, trials and jobs, oracles that validate your setup before you spend tokens, and ATIF trajectories. Then he shows how his team runs Harbor at scale on Daytona and with Phoenix to test a prompt change that steered agents toward a new SQL tool, cutting tool calls without hurting correctness.

episodes.title: How to Build an AI Code Review Agent - Daksh Gupta, Greptile
episodes.description:
Daksh Gupta, co-founder of Greptile, which reviews about 1% of all pull requests on GitHub, shares what Greptile tells companies that want to build their own review agent. Starting from a simple sandbox-plus-webhook setup, he explains why it misses bugs, costs $3-25 per PR and floods you with nitpicks, then walks through the fixes: targeted prompts, a dataset of past incident PRs, model inversion (reviewing Claude-written code with GPT and vice versa catches about 10% more bugs), codebase context and a living wiki, autonomous testing in sandboxes with computer use, and routing cheaper models to most subtasks.

episodes.title: Build Your Own Team of Managed Agents - Jack Wotherspoon, Google DeepMind
episodes.description:
Jack Wotherspoon, developer experience engineer at Google DeepMind, introduces Gemini Managed Agents: coding agents that run in cloud sandboxes from a single API call instead of on your laptop. He covers the Interactions API, the Antigravity harness, environments that several agents can share, uploaded skills and AGENTS.md files, a proxy that keeps secrets out of the sandbox, scheduled triggers and multi-agent workflows. Demos include an SEC filing researcher handing its work to a quant agent, and a stock research app built in AI Studio.

episodes.title: How to Build Voice Agents That Don't Fall Apart When You Interrupt - Jesse Hall, LiveKit
episodes.description:
Jesse Hall of LiveKit shows how to build voice agents for financial services that feel human, not robotic. He explains why model leaderboards mislead (they score components, but you ship a conversation), why you should measure time to first audio and time to first sentence instead of first byte or first token, and how async tool calls keep a conversation flowing while slow back-end work runs. He also covers audio-aware turn detection, the roughly 1.5-second latency budget (500-600ms feels truly human), and benchmarking your own stack with simulated callers.

episodes.title: How to Write Your First AI Eval - SallyAnn DeLucia, Arize AI
episodes.description:
A hands-on workshop from SallyAnn DeLucia, head of product at Arize AI, on moving from vibe checks to real evals. She covers what an eval is and how it differs from a unit test, the main types (LLM as a judge, decision models, code evals, annotations, agent as a judge), how to read a trace, how to write concrete pass/fail criteria, and how to build and iterate on an LLM judge in Arize's prompt playground.

episodes.title: What Does an AI Engineer Do Now? - Aparna Dhinakaran, Arize AI
episodes.description:
Aparna Dhinakaran of Arize AI revisits what an AI engineer actually does as the field moves from writing features to running factories of agents. The job now is building the loop: evals that review non-deterministic work, telemetry that agents consume, and agents that act on it. She walks through how Arize built Signal, an always-on agent that reads traces, remembers past issues and opens PRs, covering triggers, sandboxes, durable state, and evaluating the evaluators.

episodes.title: Can Your AI Analyst Keep a Secret? - Aaron Linsky, Bridgewater & Nikhil Benesch, turbopuffer
episodes.description:
An AI analyst at a firm like Bridgewater needs private documents, but every email, memo and research note carries its own permissions. Aaron Linsky (head of product engineering, Bridgewater Associates) explains why the Vault's 100 million permissioned documents broke their first search setup, and Nikhil Benesch (CTO, turbopuffer) breaks down the fix: post-filtering loses recall, pre-filtering is too slow, and "native filtering" over a clustered vector index gets both, delivering about 120ms P90 searches across 400 million vectors.

episodes.title: How to Build Financial Agents That Work Across the Web - Jay Sahnan & Arik Bird, Browserbase
episodes.description:
Some of the most important financial data sits behind logins and anti-bot walls, with no API. Jay Sahnan and Arik Bird of Browserbase show how browser agents solve this through three case studies: Ramp fetching receipts at scale (over 30,000 manual hours saved), Bill paying across thousands of different vendor portals with one agent, and Stripe automating KYC checks. They also cover how Browserbase forked Chromium to run reliably in the cloud, and how Stagehand's act, extract and observe primitives keep automations from breaking when sites change.

episodes.title: Do Not Let Models Invent Numbers - Vinoo Ganesh, Kepler
episodes.description:
In finance, you never show a figure you can't trace. Vinoo Ganesh, CEO of Kepler (previously Palantir and Citadel), explains Kepler's architecture where models cite numbers but never write them: retrieval finds the source, deterministic code does the math, and a post-processing filter strips any figure that can't be verified. He covers the citation registry built from more than 30 million SEC documents, hybrid search and re-ranking on turbopuffer, tenant isolation, and why plain RAG produced thousands of wrong numbers in their evals.
